extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students and instructors learning how to read and write proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory textbook guidance for reading and constructing mathematical proofs using a keyword-indexed taxonomy of techniques and a recursive algorithm for applying them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forward-Backward Method
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine forward reasoning from the hypotheses with backward reasoning from the goal and 'meet in the middle.' This is the default method for most statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward: from hypotheses, derive consequences. Backward: from the goal, identify what would suffice. Use both directions and aim to connect them. No specific anti-patterns listed, but implied: don't only pursue one direction if a meeting-in-the-middle approach is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction Method
rubrics_metrics.description: Used when the statement contains 'there exists x such that P(x)'; find an explicit x and verify P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trigger: existential claims ('there exists'). Template: exhibit an explicit object (or give a rule to construct it) and then check the desired property. Guidance: apply the construction template directly; avoid assuming existence without giving a construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose Method
rubrics_metrics.description: Triggered by universal quantifiers 'for every x, P(x)'; let x be arbitrary of the relevant type and prove P(x) without using any special property of x beyond its type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trigger: universal claims. Template: introduce an arbitrary element and prove the property for it. Anti-pattern: using properties that only hold for some special x (i.e., not truly arbitrary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying a universal ('for every') hypothesis to a specific element, substitute that element into the hypothesis and use the consequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trigger: having a 'for every' hypothesis and a need to use it on a particular object. Template: substitute the specific object to obtain the stated consequent. Guidance: this is the standard way to get concrete information from universal statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradiction Method
rubrics_metrics.description: When no direct path is visible, assume the negation of the conclusion and derive a falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trigger: difficulty finding a direct argument. Template: assume ¬(conclusion), then derive a contradiction (often using hypotheses or known facts). Notes: useful when direct forward/backward steps stall; be careful to show the contradiction clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive Method
rubrics_metrics.description: For an implication P ⇒ Q, prove the equivalent contrapositive ¬Q ⇒ ¬P when that direction is easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trigger: implication statements where the contrapositive is simpler. Template: restate the goal as the contrapositive and prove it. Guidance: only use when it genuinely simplifies reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness Method
rubrics_metrics.description: Triggered by 'there exists a unique x'; prove existence and then assume two such objects and show they are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trigger: uniqueness claims. Template: split into existence proof (often construction) and uniqueness proof: assume x and y both satisfy the property and show x = y. Guidance: both parts are necessary for 'unique existence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Triggered by statements 'for all n in N, P(n)'; prove a base case and an inductive step. Use strong induction when the inductive step requires assuming P(k) for all k ≤ n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trigger: universal claims over the natural numbers. Template: base case then show P(n) ⇒ P(n+1) (or use strong induction). Guidance: choose ordinary vs strong induction depending on what the step requires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Either-Or Method (Case Analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Triggered by a disjunctive hypothesis P ∨ Q; split into two cases and handle each separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trigger: disjunctions in hypotheses or the structure of the goal. Template: prove the conclusion in each case and conclude it holds generally. Guidance: ensure cases cover all possibilities and are handled distinctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Max/Min Method
rubrics_metrics.description: Used for claims about extreme (maximum or minimum) elements: show every element ≤ the proposed max and show the proposed max is achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trigger: statements asserting an element is maximal/minimal or about extrema. Template: demonstrate both extremal bounding and existence/achievement. Guidance: often involves constructing or identifying an element that attains the extremum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solow's Algorithm for Doing a Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A step-by-step procedure: (1) identify keywords in the statement, (2) match them to the indicated technique, (3) apply the template of that technique, (4) recursively apply the algorithm to resulting sub-goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat proof construction as partly mechanical pattern-recognition: scan for trigger words (e.g., 'there exists', 'for every', 'if...then', 'unique', 'for all n'), choose the corresponding method, use the method's standard template, and when new sub-goals arise, repeat. Guidance: recursion—apply the same keyword-technique mapping to sub-goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading a Proof as a Sequence of Techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof should be read as a sequence of applied techniques; good reading identifies which technique was used at each step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice: label each paragraph or step with its technique (e.g., 'Construction step', 'Forward step', 'Specialization'). Guidance: this labeling trains recognition and aids comprehension of the proof's structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Proof Criterion: Use techniques triggered by the statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'good proof' uses techniques whose triggers are present in the statement being proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether each technique used corresponds to an explicit or implicit trigger in the statement. Anti-pattern: invoking techniques that lack any trigger in the statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Proof Criterion: Apply each technique by its standard template
rubrics_metrics.description: Each technique applied should follow the standard template for that technique (e.g., show base case and inductive step for induction; exhibit an object for constructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring guidance: check that the canonical steps of the chosen method are present and correctly executed rather than improvised or incomplete variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Proof Criterion: Make the technique in use obvious (labeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: A good proof labels or makes clear which technique is in use at each step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: either explicitly state the kind of step ('We now construct...','Assume for contradiction...') or structure the prose so the technique is evident. This improves readability and pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Proof Criterion: Don't invoke a technique without its trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using a proof technique unless the statement contains the appropriate trigger for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: using existential reasoning without constructing an example, or applying induction without a natural number structure present. Ensure method choice is justified by the statement's form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Proof Criterion: Ensure sub-goals are provable by the same algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: The sub-goals produced while following a technique should themselves be approachable by the same keyword-to-technique algorithm (recursively solvable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether sub-goals reduce to cases with identifiable triggers and standard templates; if a sub-goal lacks triggers, reconsider earlier choices.
